turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell turned to Gwendolen and asked, 'Tell me, dear, have you any idea where this young man's house is?'

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen called up to the drawing room, asking if she could come up now

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack asked if he might be excused for a moment, feeling a bit overwhelmed by Lady Bracknell's intense questioning

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that she would not tolerate any further frivolity and insisted that he provide a satisfactory explanation for his claim to be Gwendolen's cousin.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he had, in fact, met Gwendolen under rather unusual circumstances, but he was convinced that she genuinely believed he was her cousin and he had not seen any reason to correct her.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's tone turned disapproving as she asked, 'And pray, Mr. Worthing, how long did this...ahem...mistaken identity persist?'

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack's eyes dropped, his fingers nervously fidgeting with his gloves as he inquired, 'If I may, Lady Bracknell, I believe it was only when I met Miss Gwendolen that I realized my... confusion.'

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell raised an eyebrow and told Jack that she was not aware of any gentleman being expected to acknowledge confusion, and that it was a most ungentlemanly sentiment to express.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he was not trying to be ungentlemanly, but was simply stating the obvious, as he was indeed confused about his identity as Ernest Worple.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that his explanation was patently absurd and that he seemed to be making a mockery of the institution of marriage.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained, with a slightly nervous tone, that he was simply trying to be honest about his circumstances, and that he hoped Lady Bracknell could understand his position.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell raised an eyebrow, her expression skeptical, and told Jack that she was not interested in excuses, but in facts, and that he was expected to provide her with some explanation for his unusual surname.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that the name was a family name, passed down from his great-aunt, and that he had never given it much thought before.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell raised an eyebrow, her voice dripping with skepticism as she told Jack that his casual explanation was hardly reassuring and that he should have given more thought to the implications of his name.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he had never given much thought to the implications of his name, and that it had simply been given to him by his parents, but he was willing to change it if it caused any trouble for his fiancée or her mother.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen insisted that she knew her own mind and that she would not be influenced by her mother's objections to her fiancé's name.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he had always been called Jack by his family and friends, and that he did not think it was a matter of great importance.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that she was astonished that he would trivialize something as significant as his given name, and that she expected him to be more mindful of the dignity and propriety expected of a suitor for her daughter's hand.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack expressed his apologies for any offense he may have caused, explaining that he had never intended to diminish the importance of his given name, and that he was willing to do whatever it took to prove himself a suitable husband for Gwendolen.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell asked Gwendolen to ensure that she was indeed in a suitable frame of mind to be married to this man, given his dubious background and questionable character.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen told Lady Bracknell that she was engaged to Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Gwendolen and Mr. Worthing to pardon her, as they were not engaged to anyone. She explained that when they did become engaged, she or Mr. Worthing's father, if his health permitted, would inform them of the fact. An engagement should come as a surprise to a young girl, and it was hardly a matter she could arrange for herself. While she was making inquiries, Gwendolen would wait for her below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen called out to Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Gwendolen to wait for her in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen replied to Lady Bracknell that she would wait for her.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Mr. Worthing to take a seat.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack stood tall, his eyes locked on Lady Bracknell, and said that he preferred to remain standing, rather than take a seat.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell informed Mr. Worthing that he was not on her list of eligible young men, although she had the same list as the Duchess of Bolton. However, she was willing to enter his name if his answers were satisfactory. She asked him if he smoked.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing admitted to Lady Bracknell that he smoked.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing smoked. She believed that a man should have an occupation. There were too many idle men in London. She asked Mr. Worthing how old he was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he was twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that twenty-nine was a good age to get married. She believed that a man who wanted to get married should know either everything or nothing. She asked Mr. Worthing which category he fell into.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that he knew nothing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing knew nothing. She believed that ignorance was a delicate and exotic fruit that should not be tampered with. She stated that education was unsound and produced no effect in England. If it did, it would be a danger to the upper classes. She asked Mr. Worthing about his income.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his income was between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing if his income came from land or investments.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that his income came from investments.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that Mr. Worthing's income was satisfactory. She stated that land was no longer a profit or pleasure, but rather a means of gaining position and losing it. She asked Mr. Worthing about his country house.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he had a country house with some land, but he did not depend on it for his income. In fact, the poachers were the only ones who made anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing how many bedrooms his country house had. She also asked if he had a town house, as a girl like Gwendolen could not be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he owned a house in Belgrave Square, but it was let by the year to Lady Bloxham.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing who Lady Bloxham was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack observed that Lady Bracknell went out very little, and that she was a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing what number his house in Belgrave Square was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his house was number 149.
